evidence: Cic. Inv. 2.160: intellegentia est, per quam animus ea perspicit, quae sunt (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The power of discerning and understanding (Lewis & Short). The adjective is intellegēns.
Inborn talent and quickness of mind, as against learning (see ability). Its first sense is a person’s nature or character (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Brut. 49 (by chapter): semperne vulgī jūdicium cum intellegentium jūdiciō congruit? (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of a person who understands a matter; as a noun, an expert, a connoisseur (Lewis & Short). For a quick or clever person see clever.
First perception by the senses (Pliny), then understanding (Quintilian, Seneca).

phrases.latin: intellegentia est, per quam animus ea perspicit, quae sunt
phrases.english: intelligence is the power by which the mind sees clearly the things that are

phrases.latin: manent ingenia senibus, modo permaneat studium et industria
phrases.english: the old keep their wits, as long as they keep their interest and their diligence
